source.title: Large Language Models as Detectors or Instigators of Hate Speech in Low-resource Ethiopian Languages
source.authors: Nuhu Ibrahim; Felicity Mulford; R. Batista-Navarro

record.tranche_reason: The study compares few-shot downstream detection performance across model sizes and reports that larger models do not consistently perform better, particularly in Ethiopian languages. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Rows record the hate-speech detection F1 results by model and language. The generation results are not rows for V6: the models were explicitly prompted to produce hate speech, and the study does not report a scale-related downstream-performance measure for that induced behavior. The study also reports precision, recall and accuracy, but the F1 table is the principal measure used in its discussion of model-size patterns.
record.test_reason: The study compares off-the-shelf models of different sizes on few-shot hate-speech detection and explicitly argues against the assumption that larger models consistently perform better, citing Kaplan et al. Its own results bear on V6, but weakly. No controlled scaling sweep was run. Larger LLaMA 3 and Mistral checkpoints are 4-bit quantised, while the smaller ones are not. In the Ethiopian languages every model sits near chance accuracy (43–54%). No loss or fit is measured, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say larger models perform better on monolingual English but not on Ethiopian languages or code-mixed English, where bigger models often do worse. They also attribute the drops of the quantised LLaMA 3 12B/70B and Mistral-13B models to quantisation, which undercuts reading those drops as a size effect. Separately, they report that all models can be prompted to generate profiled hate speech.
record.recipe_differences: This is a few-shot downstream hate-speech detection benchmark across models and languages, not a pretraining loss sweep, scaling-law fit, extrapolation test or compute-allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Language category changes the reported model-size pattern. Quantisation is also associated with degraded performance in low-resource languages, but it is confounded with some of the larger model comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: 4-bit quantisation of larger checkpoints coincides with sharp drops in low-resource and code-mixed detection but not in monolingual English. Several quantised models collapse to near-zero recall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight quantisation degrades downstream performance disproportionately in low-resource languages.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 9th Widening NLP Workshop
record.problems: The evaluation uses few-shot prompting and 1,000 labelled posts per language. Model sizes are not presented as a controlled scaling sweep; several larger models are quantised, and the paper notes that quantisation may explain some performance drops. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors also state that prompts were written in English, which may have affected cross-lingual results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Table 2 also reports precision, recall and accuracy; the F1 results are retained because the paper uses F1 to discuss model performance patterns and the 50-row limit precludes duplicating all metrics.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss; any fitted or smooth scaling trend; controlled size sweeps within one family at fixed precision; tasks other than few-shot binary hate-speech detection.
Not tested: no pretraining loss measured.
Not tested: no extrapolation of fitted laws.
Not tested: no other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: no fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Accuracy values, which show every model at roughly chance (43–54%) in the Ethiopian languages. This is needed to read the F1 size comparisons, which reflect recall bias. Example: Mistral-7B has 100% recall on Amharic at 51.4% accuracy.

Several LLaMA 3-12B* rows duplicate DeepSeek-7B rows exactly (Tigrigna and M-English on all metrics; Amharic matches DeepSeek's Afaan Oromo row). The model is also called 13B elsewhere, and Qwen-14B is absent from the model list in Sec 2.2. Table 2 may be corrupted.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence on V6 is weak. The models are released checkpoints, not a sweep, and size is confounded with 4-bit quantisation for the LLaMA and Mistral comparisons. The Ethiopian-language results are at chance for every model, so F1 differences mostly reflect output label bias. Table 2 likely contains copy errors. The generation results involve induced behaviour and are correctly excluded. Tranche is T5 because the authors explicitly argue against size-based improvement, citing Kaplan et al.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning or transfer.
The study tests few-shot hate-speech detection across models and languages, not a general downstream scaling relation, prediction from pretraining loss, or other downstream tasks.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and sensitivity to scaling-law fit choices.

rows.subject: LLaMA 3-12B*
rows.operation_detail: Compared six-shot detection F1 with the smaller reported LLaMA 3 model.

rows.check: Unquantised 8B is compared with 4-bit 12B*, so size is confounded with quantisation. Accuracy rises 44.8→53.9, but both are near chance. The 12B* value 57.90 duplicates DeepSeek-7B's Amharic F1, a possible table error. The paper calls this model 13B in Sec 2.2 and Appendix C.

rows.operation_detail: Compared six-shot detection F1 with the smaller reported LLaMA 3 model.
rows.note: The larger model has much lower F1; both compared models are quantised.
rows.check: Both models are quantised. Accuracy stays at chance (53.9→46.5). The F1 fall comes from recall collapsing to 6.4, a degenerate output bias rather than a capability change.

relationships.condition: Monolingual English, within the LLaMA 3, Mistral and Qwen families
relationships.reason: F1 and accuracy rise with size: LLaMA 12B*→70B* (R45), Mistral 7B→13B* (R47), Qwen 1.8B→7B→14B (R49, R50). These are few models, not a controlled sweep.
relationships.display_finding: F1 and accuracy increased from LLaMA 12B* to 70B*, Mistral 7B to 13B*, and Qwen 1.8B to 7B to 14B.

relationships.condition: Afaan Oromo, Amharic and Tigrigna, in unquantised Qwen comparisons and quantised LLaMA 12B*→70B* comparisons
relationships.reason: Accuracy stays at chance (about 36–54%) at every size, with no improvement from scale (R09, R10, R19, R20, R29, R30, R05, R15, R25).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy remained at chance, about 36–54%, across the tested sizes in all three languages.

relationships.reason: Qwen accuracy rises only slightly near chance and its F1 is non-monotonic (R39, R40). Quantised LLaMA 70B* falls below 12B* (R35), with recall collapsing to 5.8.
relationships.display_finding: Qwen accuracy improved only slightly near chance with nonmonotonic F1, while quantized LLaMA 70B* underperformed 12B* and recall fell to 5.8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: M-English, within the reported LLaMA 3, Mistral and Qwen size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: F1 rises across the reported sizes in each of these model families for M-English (R43–R50). The models are not a controlled scaling sweep, and some larger checkpoints are quantised.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Ethiopian-language and C-English comparisons involving larger LLaMA 3 or Mistral checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The larger reported checkpoint has lower F1 in these comparisons; the larger checkpoints are quantised, so the results challenge straightforward size-based predictability but do not isolate size from quantisation (R04–R07, R14–R17, R24–R27, R34–R37).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Qwen size comparisons across the five language categories
reader_labels.reason: Qwen F1 falls at 7B and rises again at 14B in the four non-M-English categories, rather than following a consistently increasing pattern (R08–R10, R18–R20, R28–R30, R38–R40).
